title: Wanderer
editorial_note: Source body duplicates the title-variant record “If the Leaf-Fall's Disasters Find You Thoughtful...” and is retained here under its supplied title.

title: Six Months Dead Already! And in Vain I Have Tried
text:
Six months dead already! And in vain I have tried

for a kiss, a word, a breath, a sound…

and despite my faith, each day I prove

that behind the grave there is nothing but silence…


If I had died, what seas, what cataclysms,

what vertices, what mists, what peaks and what abysses

would mock my fevered, all-powerful desire

to come at night and kiss you on the forehead,

to descend with the light of a prophetic star,

to say in your ear: Do not forget me.


And you, who perhaps loved me more than I loved you,

are inexorably silent, so that I know no more

than to doubt everything, the soul, destiny,

and to set myself weeping in the middle of the road!

For with infinite desolation I prove

that behind the grave there is nothing but silence…
editorial_note: The translation preserves the elegiac address and the repeated conclusion that beyond the grave there is only silence.

title: The Child Heroes of Chapultepec
text:
Like shoots whose fresh adornments
a freezing north wind destroys in bloom,
so fell the child heroes
before the invader's bullets.


Fleeting as a dream, the span
of their ideal childhood
was; but Glory, immortal mother,
lulled them in her lap.


Soon the beloved homeland
needed their lives,
and one after another, life
they smilingly gave her.


On the laughing hill
of the Forest, one following another,
they fell, with the divine
majesty of a young god.


Who, after hearing tell
of such pious offering,
would deny the Homeland
the blood she gave him?


Childhood that found a Calvary
at life's dawn:
may the tricolor flag
serve you as a shroud.


And may heaven and earth
sing your deeds without cease,
the condor of the mountains
and the waves of the sea…
editorial_note: The translation preserves the patriotic elegy, Chapultepec, and the tricolor flag as a shroud.

title: Immortality
text:
No, our love's story was not so fleeting:
among the smooth pages
of the virgin book of your memory,
like a blue petal lies the glory,
sorrowful, noble, and chaste, of my verses.


You cannot forget me: I condemn you
to a tenacious memory. My love has been
the highest thing in your life, the best;
and only amid mud and mire
does the pale lotus of oblivion arise.


You will see me everywhere: in the uncertain
evening, in the blond dawn,
and when you work in the deserted
corridor, while in your garden tremble
the monotonous threads of rain.


And you will have to remember! That is the inheritance
my pain gives you, which nothing can soothe.
I will be a summit of light in your existence,
and an ineffable reproach in your conscience
and an immortal wake within your soul!
editorial_note: The translation keeps the prophetic address and recurring memory, lotus, and immortal-trace imagery.

title: The Shadow of the Wing
text:
You who think I do not believe
when we argue, the two of us,
do not imagine my desire,
my thirst, my hunger for God;


nor have you heard my cry
of despair, which fills
the entrails of darkness
invoking the Infinite;


nor do you see my thought,
which, bent on producing
an ideal, often suffers
the tortures of childbirth.


If my barren spirit
had your fertility,
it would already have forged a heaven
to complete its world.


But tell me, what effort can there be
in a soul without a flag
that carries everywhere
your torturer—who knows?;


that lives fasting from faith
and, with tenacious heroism,
goes asking every abyss
and every night a why?


In every case, my thirst
for investigation shields me,
my deep and silent thirst for God;
and there is more love in my doubt
than in your tepid affirmation.
editorial_note: The source punctuation around “tu torturador ¿quién sabe?” is syntactically irregular and remains marked in English.

title: I Don't Know Who She Is
text:
Who is she? —I don't know: sometimes she crosses

my path, like the fairy

of dreaming: always alone…

always mute… always pale…

Her name? I do not know it.

Where does she come from? Where is she going?

I do not know! We meet,

she looks at me a moment and passes:

Always alone… Always sad…

Always mute… Always pale!


Woman: for a long time I have carried

your image inside my soul.

If the shadows that surround you,

if the mysteries you keep

must be impenetrable

to everyone, hush, hush!


I ask only for love:

I ask you nothing!


Are you seeking rest and oblivion?

So am I. The world grows weary.

We will leave far, far away

from people, to a strange land;

and like birds that nest

in solitary towers,

we will entrust to the shadow

our love and our longings…
editorial_note: The translation preserves the repeated portrait of the unknown woman and the invitation into exile.

title: Jesus
text:
Jesus did not come from the world of “the heavens.”
He came from the very depths of souls;
from where the self nests: from the inner
regions of the Spirit.


Why seek him above the clouds?
Clouds are not the throne of gods.
Why seek him in the burning stars?
They are flames like the sun that lights us,
orbs of inflamed gases… Only flames.
Why seek him on the planets?
They are globes like ours, lit
by a star around which they revolve.


Jesus came from where
the deepest thoughts
and the most remote instinct come.
He did not descend: he emerged from the endless
ocean of the subconscious;
he returned to it, and there he is, serene and pure.
He was and is a lion. Whoever ventures
boldly into the abyss
without shores of himself,
with the light of love, finds him.
editorial_note: The translation preserves Nervo’s interior account of Jesus and his emergence from the subconscious.

title: One with Him
text:
You are one with God, because you love Him.
What does your smallness matter, your misery?
You are one with God, because you love Him!


You sought Him in the books,
you sought Him in the temples,
you sought Him in the stars,


and one day the heart told you, trembling:
“Here He is,” and since then you are one,
you are both one, because you love Him.


Nothing could separate you,
neither the pleasure of life
nor the pain of death.


In pleasure you must look at His face,
in pain you must look at His face,
in life and death you must look at His face.


“God!” you will say in kisses,
you will say “God” in songs,
you will say “God!” in groans.


And understanding at last that all sin
(like all life) is illusory,
and that nothing can separate you from Him,
you will feel one with God forever:
one alone with God, because you love Him.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the devotional address, repeated “face,” and final union with God.

title: So Much Love
text:
There is so much love in my soul that no room remains
not even the narrowest corner for hate.
Where do you want me to put the resentments
that your vilenesses might engender?


I am not impassive: I feel everything,
I suffer everything… But like the child
whom they make cry, as soon as he sees
a toy before his eyes
he consoles himself, smiles,
and stretches his eager hands
toward it without remembering the pain,
so I, before the divine panorama
of my idea, before the ineffable
of my infinite love,
feel neither the evil pinprick
nor the cruel sharp
irony, nor hear the sarcastic
laughter. I forget everything,
because I am only heart, only eyes
nothing more, to lean from the window
and watch the ineffable Dream pass,
dressed in violet,
and with all the light of morning
in his divine eyes, in the quiet
clarity of the fountain…
editorial_note: The translation preserves the child-and-toy comparison and the violet-clad Dream at the fountain. The source compresses “todo…Pero” without a following space; the English restores the sentence spacing.

title: Sometimes, in Dreams, My Spirit Pretends...
text:
Sometimes, in dreams, my spirit pretends

scenes from distant lives:

I was

an Egyptian satrap with a sphinx-like face,

wearing a golden miter, and I lived in Memphis.


Once dead, my soul continued its erratic flight,

wearing in Jerusalem, and unfaithful to Osiris,

the two-horned miter and the hieratic ephod

of the great priest of the God of Israel.


Then I raised my prayers with the druid

and in sacred forest Velleda loved me.

I was a Merovingian king with a flowering beard;

an iron crown encircled my brow.


Later, troubadour of noble feudal lords,

I sang their deeds, their feats of honor,

I ate at their table, and at a thousand bacchanals

felt myself drunk with wine and love.

And yesterday, an austere, elusive prior,


I brought my trembling lips to the Eucharistic God:

therefore I preserve pious traces,

and seek retreat, following the sages,

and suffer immense nostalgias for faith.
editorial_note: The source punctuation is compressed in “Y ayer, prior esquivo y austero los labios / al Dios eucarístico, temblando acerqué”; the translation reads it as the speaker, an austere and elusive prior, bringing trembling lips to the Eucharistic God.

title: For Many Years I Have Sought the Wilderness...
text:
For many years I have sought the wilderness,

for many years I have lived sadly,

for many years I have been ill,

and it is because of the book you wrote!


O Kempis, before reading you I loved

the light, the meadows, the Ocean Sea;

but you said that everything ends,

that everything dies, that everything is vain!


Before, carried by my desires,

I kissed lips that invite a kiss,

the blond braids, the large eyes,

without remembering that they wither!


But since grave doctors affirm,

whom you, master, cite and name,

that man passes like ships,

like clouds, like shadows…


I flee every earthly bond,

no affection gladdens my mind,

and with your book under my arm

I go traversing the black night…


O Kempis, Kempis, barren ascetic,

pale ascetic, how you harmed me!

For many years I have been ill,

and it is because of the book you wrote!
editorial_note: The translation preserves the playful accusation against Kempis and the repeated refrain about the book that made the speaker ill.

title: Each Gentle Rose Born Yesterday...
text:
Each gentle rose born yesterday,

each dawn that rises among blushes,

leaves my soul sunk in ecstasy…

My eyes never tire of gazing

at life's perpetual miracle!


For years I have contemplated the stars

on transparent Spanish nights

and find them ever more beautiful.

For years, alone with me upon the sea,

I hear from the waves their laments

and still the prodigy of waves amazes me!


Every time I find Nature

more supernatural, purer and holier.

For me, all around, everything is beauty:

and with the same fullness it delights me,

the mother's mouth when she prays

as the child's mouth when he sings.


I want to be immortal, with intense thirst,

because the panorama

that immense creation offers us is wonderful;

because every star calls me,

saying as it shines: “Here one thinks,

here too one struggles, here one loves!”.
editorial_note: Source body is nearly identical to “Ecstasy”; its unaccented “mas” does not alter the English translation.

editorial_note: Source body is nearly identical to “Each Gentle Rose Born Yesterday...”; it differs chiefly in accenting “más.”

title: Who Is That Siren with Such a Sorrowful Voice...
text:
Who is that siren with such sorrowful voice,

with flesh so white, with braid so brown?

—It is a ray of moonlight bathing in the fountain,

it is a ray of moonlight…


Who, crying my name, crosses the dwelling?

Who calls me at night in such trembling tones?

—It is a breath of wind sobbing in the tower,

it is a breath of wind…


Tell me, who are you, archangel whose wings burn

in the divine fire of evening, and you rise

through the glory of ether?

—They are the clouds that pass;

look closely, they are the clouds…


Who spilled her necklaces in the water, my God?

They are rain of diamonds on blue velvet.

—It is heaven's image pulsing in the river,

it is heaven's image…


O Lord! Beauty is only, then, a mirage!

Nothing but You are certain: be my last Master.

Where to find You—in the ether, in the earth, in myself?

—A little dream will guide you through each abyss,

a little dream…
editorial_note: The translation preserves the poem’s question-and-answer structure, shifting each apparition into moonlight, wind, clouds, heaven, and dream.

title: More Than Myself
text:
O my life, my life!,
I agonized with your agony
and died with your death.
I loved you so much
that being without you is being without me!


Lighthouse of my devotion,
everlasting as my affliction
is your blessed memory.
Sweet and holy little lamp
within my heart!


Light that illumines my sorrow
since you departed
and will illumine it to the end,
for if you left me sad,
sad you will find me.


And when I bow my head,
forever and ever,
the illness that begins to gnaw at me,
I think that by my sadness
you will recognize me.


By virtue of the noble radiance
of memory, my pain
will be a mirror in which you must see yourself,
and thus love's clarity
will conquer death.


There will be neither carriage nor abyss
that weakens my heroism
of seeking you without cease.
If you were more than I myself,
how could I fail to find you?


O my life, my life!,
I agonized with your agony
and died with your death!
I loved you so much,
that being without you is being without me.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the repeated death-and-memory refrain and the speaker’s conviction that love’s clarity defeats death.

title: Friend, My Lararium Is Empty
text:
Friend, my lararium is empty:

since the hearth fire no longer burns,

our gods fled before the cold;

today tedium presides on their thrones

over the nuptials of silence and evening.


Destructive time does not pass in vain;

the courtyard eaves are in ruins;

the swallows no longer form there

their delicate house, with convex walls of mortar

and down for a tapestry.


What silence at the piano! Its moan

no longer vibrates in deserted spaces;

the nocturnes and scherzos have fled…

Poor cage without birds! Poor nest!

Mysterious coffin of dead trills!


Ah, if you could see your garden! No roses now,

nor lilies, nor silk-winged dragonflies,

nor fireflies of light, nor butterflies…

The rosebush branches tremble, frightened;

the wind blows, leaf litter rolls.


Friend, your mansion is deserted;

the black-green moss that adorns

the ruined lintels of the door

seems an inscription that says: Dead!

The north wind passes, and sighing: Weep!
editorial_note: The translation preserves the domestic shrine, ruined garden, silent piano, and final inscription of mourning.

title: Let Us Adore the Ivory Flesh...
text:
Let us adore ivory flesh,

let us gild faces of archaic profiles,

aristocratic treasure;

foreheads bathed in pale gold,

hands with elongated phalanges,

where noble blood runs blue.


Come, let us adore

the arcane Ideal, companions.


Let us adore dilated eyes,

steeped, like a sea of shadows,

in diaphanous and astral clarities,

eyes that hysteria brightens,

eyes that by day are abyss,

eyes that by night are beacons.


Come, let us adore

the arcane Ideal, companions.


Let us adore souls forever aloof,

the most silent, the strange,

that never dissolve into loves:

urn-souls of immense desolations,

that rise intact to the heavens,

or sink intact into Cocytus.


Come, let us adore

the arcane Ideal, companions.


O poets, exalted lovers

of the arcane Ideal, rulers

of rebellious form: let us labor

to rebuild the Gothic altars,

and then to their protective shadows

come, let us adore!
editorial_note: The translation keeps the incantatory refrain and the poem’s decadent catalogue of the arcane Ideal.

title: For a Long Time I Dreamed of You
text:
For a long time I dreamed of you

thus, dressed in white tulle,

and to my soul that sought you,

I asked, Ana, what do you see?

as in Bluebeard's tale.


For a long time I sensed

your black eyes as I saw them,

and in my hours of nostalgia,

Sister Anne answered me:

“There is a virgin coming to you.”


And glimpsing you, feverish, awake,

behind the tower's ogive,

after having moved uncertainly,

like a bell that tolls for the dead,

my heart tolled for glory.


At last, different, you appeared to me;

reveille calls rang around,

the sad Muse silently fled

and you arrived, saw, and conquered

like the magnificent Emperor.


Today, my hope that runs toward you,

that looks to the sky where you may be,

because glory is unveiled to it,

no longer asks from the tower:

Sister Anne, tell me, what do you see?


Today in my night your light reigns,

I see your face shine,

and in my dreams I only wish

to raise you like a flag

and, embracing you, to conquer through you!
editorial_note: The translation preserves the Bluebeard/Sister Anne allusion, military triumph imagery, and the final embrace.

title: The May Flower Song
text:
May Flower like a ray
of afternoon was dying…
I loved you, May Flower,
you know it; but God did not will it!


Waves come, waves go,
singing they come, singing they will go.


May Flower neither dresses
nor adorns nor arrays herself;
May Flower is very sad!
Poor little thing, poor life of mine!


Each star that pulses,
from heaven speaks to her thus:
“Come with me, little flower,
you will shine in the vastness just like me.”


May Flower, faintly,
answers: “Soon I will go!”


May Flower is dying,
May Flower, the chosen one, has gone from us!


Waves come, waves go,
singing they come, weeping they will go…


“Do not leave me!” I cry to her:
“Do not go, my mistress,
the space is infinite
and very black and cold, so cold!”


Heedless of my pleading,
May Flower moved away,
and in the night, like a dream,
mysteriously sad, was lost.


Waves come, waves go,
singing they come, ah, how will they go!


Under the shelter of my garden
only one flower grew:
May Flower, and she has died…
I loved her, but God did not will it!
editorial_note: The translation preserves the refrain, personified flower, and the tension between the speaker’s love and divine will.

title: Through That Door
text:
Through that door she fled saying: “Never!”
Through that door she must return one day…
When she closed that door she left cut short
the golden thread of my hope.
Through that door she must return one day.


Each time the impulse of the breeze,
like a weak, undecided hand,
lightly shakes the window,
my coward heart awaiting her
beats faster, faster.


From my worktable I see
the door my desires dream of
and my desire lurks crouched
in the trembling depth of my eyes.


For how long, solitary, elusive,
must I wait with uncertain gaze
for God, compassionate, to return to me
the woman who fled through that door?


When will those panes tremble,
pushed by her ducal hands,
and with her kiss arrive to them,
as in winter nights there comes to me
the pious kiss of a star?
O Lord, the pale one is already alert!
O Lord, evening falls now on my road
and my dead hope freezes!
O Lord, make the door open at last
and let my beloved enter through it!…
Through that door she must return one day!
editorial_note: The translation preserves the repeated prophecy of return and the door as the central image of hope.
